summary: You established a strong rationale and identified relevant users for your Great Barrier Reef monitoring concept, presenting your work with clear structure. To improve, address critical technical details in your orbital mechanics, develop quantified mission requirements, and include concrete technical calculations rather than generic software tutorials. Additionally, strengthen your project plan with contingencies and professional formatting.
next_steps: Correct the orbital parameters in your preliminary design: a true geostationary orbit requires ~35,786 km, whereas 600 km represents low Earth orbit (LEO).
Produce concrete technical results in your next report, such as payload sizing, power budgets, or initial STK orbital simulations tailored to the mission.
Format all citations with complete bibliographic details rather than raw URLs, and add formal figure numbers and descriptive captions to visuals like Image 1.

criteria.C1: You clearly articulated the mission rationale and identified user needs for monitoring the reef. To reach Accomplished, define quantitative requirements—such as revisit rates, spectral bands, and payload mass and power constraints—and integrate supporting literature.
criteria.C2: Your task breakdown and Gantt chart in Image 1 map out the schedule well. To achieve an Accomplished level, integrate specific literature and database sources, and incorporate clear contingency planning and risk management for potential project variations.
criteria.C3: Completing STK tutorials shows familiarisation, but no mission-specific engineering calculations or simulation outputs were provided. To reach Accomplished, include initial preliminary results—such as coverage analysis, delta-v budgets, or mass estimations—with clear engineering interpretations.
criteria.C4: Your document structure is neat and readable. To reach Accomplished, ensure all visual elements like Image 1 feature formal numbering and captions, and replace raw URLs in your reference list with fully structured academic citations.
